LECTURE 45 Stage 7: NeuralForge Platform

PyTorch Training — Making Your LLM Actually Learn

From 9.9% Improvement to 55.9% — Why Full Backpropagation Changes Everything
55 min read Advanced The leap from toy to real training

Introduction: The NumPy Problem

In previous lectures, we built a complete GPT-2 model in NumPy. We implemented forward passes, computed cross-entropy loss, and even wrote a training loop. But there was a fundamental limitation: our NumPy train_step only updates about 8% of the model’s parameters — specifically the output head and token embeddings.

Why? Because computing gradients for every single parameter through the entire Transformer — through attention layers, feed-forward networks, layer norms, and residual connections — requires implementing backpropagation by hand for each operation. That is hundreds of derivative calculations, each one a potential source of bugs.

The result? Our NumPy training is barely learning:

MetricNumPy TrainingPyTorch Training
Initial Loss3.743.46
Final Loss (after training)3.37 (500 steps)1.53 (30 steps)
Loss Reduction9.9%55.9%
Random Baseline3.71 (loss when guessing randomly among ~4096 tokens)
Parameters Updated~8% (head + embeddings)100% (all parameters)
Training Speed~1 step/sec~10+ steps/sec (CPU), ~100+ (GPU)

Look at those numbers carefully. After 500 training steps, our NumPy model barely beats the random baseline (3.37 vs 3.71). Meanwhile, PyTorch reaches 1.53 in just 30 steps — that is genuine learning. The model is starting to predict the next token with real understanding, not just statistical noise.

Why This Matters: A loss of 3.37 means your model is essentially guessing. A loss of 1.53 means it has learned meaningful patterns — it can complete sentences, follow grammatical rules, and generate recognizable text. This is the difference between a toy demonstration and a real language model.

Part 1: What is PyTorch?

PyTorch is a deep learning framework created by Meta (Facebook) that does one critical thing our NumPy code cannot: it automatically computes gradients for every parameter in your model.

Think of it this way:

  • NumPy is a calculator — it does the math you tell it to do, nothing more
  • PyTorch is a calculator that also remembers every calculation it performed, so it can trace back and figure out how each input affected the output

This “remembering” is called autograd (automatic gradient computation), and it is what makes training deep neural networks practical.

Installing PyTorch

PyTorch is installed with pip, just like any other Python package:

pip install torch
Size Warning: PyTorch is a large package — approximately 500 MB to 2 GB depending on your platform and whether you install GPU support. The CPU-only version is smaller. If you are on a slow connection, be patient during the download. The good news: you only install it once.

To verify the installation:

import torch
print(f"PyTorch version: {torch.__version__}")
print(f"CUDA available: {torch.cuda.is_available()}")

Part 2: How Autograd Works

This is the most important concept in this lecture. Do not worry about the math — focus on the intuition.

The Forward Pass: Building a Computation Graph

When you perform calculations with PyTorch tensors, PyTorch secretly builds a computation graph — a record of every operation performed. Imagine you compute:

x = torch.tensor([2.0], requires_grad=True)
y = x * 3      # PyTorch records: "y = x * 3"
z = y + 1      # PyTorch records: "z = y + 1"
loss = z ** 2  # PyTorch records: "loss = z ** 2"

After this forward pass, PyTorch has an internal graph:

x (2.0) → [multiply by 3] → y (6.0) → [add 1] → z (7.0) → [square] → loss (49.0)

The Backward Pass: Computing All Gradients

When you call loss.backward(), PyTorch traverses this graph in reverse, using the chain rule of calculus to compute how much each parameter contributed to the loss:

loss.backward()
print(x.grad)  # tensor([42.0])

PyTorch computed: d(loss)/dx = d(z²)/dz × dz/dy × dy/dx = 2z × 1 × 3 = 2(7) × 3 = 42.

You did not have to derive that formula. PyTorch did it automatically. Now scale this up to a model with millions of parameters and hundreds of operations — PyTorch computes all the gradients in one backward() call.

The Key Insight: In our NumPy model, we manually computed gradients for the output head and embeddings. We could not compute gradients for attention weights, FFN layers, or layer norms without writing hundreds of lines of derivative code. PyTorch’s autograd handles all of this automatically, which means every single parameter gets updated during training.

The Optimizer Step: Updating Parameters

Once gradients are computed, the optimizer uses them to update every parameter:

# After loss.backward() computes all gradients:
optimizer.step()  # Update every parameter: param = param - lr * param.grad
optimizer.zero_grad()  # Reset gradients for the next step

This three-step dance — forward, backward, step — is the heartbeat of all deep learning training.

Part 3: Converting Our Model to PyTorch

Our PyTorch model has the exact same architecture as our NumPy model. Same number of layers, same attention mechanism, same feed-forward network. The only difference is the implementation framework — which enables full gradient computation.

The nn.Module Pattern

Every PyTorch model inherits from nn.Module. This gives it the ability to:

  • Automatically track all parameters (weights and biases)
  • Move to GPU with a single .to('cuda') call
  • Save and load with torch.save() and torch.load()
  • Switch between training and evaluation modes

PyTorch Building Blocks We Use

manual mean/variance calcnn.LayerNorm(d_model)Layer normalization
np.maximum(0, x) or gelu(x)F.gelu(x)GELU activation function
np.exp(x) / sumF.softmax(x, dim=-1)Softmax (numerically stable)
-np.log(probs[target])F.cross_entropy(logits, targets)Cross-entropy loss

Weight Tying

One important optimization in modern language models: the output head shares weights with the token embedding. This is called weight tying.

Why does this make sense? The token embedding converts token IDs into vectors. The output head converts vectors back into token probabilities. These are inverse operations — so sharing the same weight matrix makes the model learn a more consistent representation.

# In practice, weight tying looks like this:
self.token_embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)
# ... later, in the forward pass:
logits = x @ self.token_embedding.weight.T  # Reuse embedding weights as output head

This also reduces the total parameter count — the embedding matrix is often the largest single weight matrix in the model.

Part 4: The Complete PyTorch Model

The model class below is a direct translation of our NumPy GPT-2 into PyTorch. Every component maps one-to-one:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import math

class MiniGPT2Torch(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, d_model, n_heads, n_layers, max_seq_len, d_ff=None):
        super().__init__()
        self.d_model = d_model
        self.n_heads = n_heads
        self.n_layers = n_layers
        self.head_dim = d_model // n_heads
        d_ff = d_ff or 4 * d_model
        
        # Token and position embeddings
        self.token_embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)
        self.position_embedding = nn.Embedding(max_seq_len, d_model)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(0.1)
        
        # Transformer layers
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([
            TransformerBlock(d_model, n_heads, d_ff)
            for _ in range(n_layers)
        ])
        
        # Final layer norm
        self.ln_f = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        
        # Weight tying: output head reuses token embedding
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(d_model, vocab_size, bias=False)
        self.lm_head.weight = self.token_embedding.weight
        
        # Initialize weights
        self.apply(self._init_weights)
    
    def _init_weights(self, module):
        if isinstance(module, nn.Linear):
            torch.nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.02)
            if module.bias is not None:
                torch.nn.init.zeros_(module.bias)
        elif isinstance(module, nn.Embedding):
            torch.nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.02)
    
    def forward(self, idx, targets=None):
        B, T = idx.shape
        
        # Embeddings
        tok_emb = self.token_embedding(idx)
        pos_emb = self.position_embedding(torch.arange(T, device=idx.device))
        x = self.drop(tok_emb + pos_emb)
        
        # Transformer layers
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x)
        
        x = self.ln_f(x)
        logits = self.lm_head(x)
        
        # Compute loss if targets provided
        loss = None
        if targets is not None:
            loss = F.cross_entropy(
                logits.view(-1, logits.size(-1)),
                targets.view(-1)
            )
        
        return logits, loss

And the Transformer block:

class TransformerBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, d_ff):
        super().__init__()
        self.ln1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.attn = CausalSelfAttention(d_model, n_heads)
        self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.ffn = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff),
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model),
            nn.Dropout(0.1),
        )
    
    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.attn(self.ln1(x))   # Residual + attention
        x = x + self.ffn(self.ln2(x))    # Residual + FFN
        return x


class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads):
        super().__init__()
        self.n_heads = n_heads
        self.head_dim = d_model // n_heads
        
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model)
        self.proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(0.1)
    
    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        
        # Compute Q, K, V in one matrix multiply
        qkv = self.qkv(x).reshape(B, T, 3, self.n_heads, self.head_dim)
        q, k, v = qkv.permute(2, 0, 3, 1, 4)  # 3 x (B, heads, T, head_dim)
        
        # Scaled dot-product attention with causal mask
        att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(self.head_dim)
        mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, device=x.device), diagonal=1).bool()
        att = att.masked_fill(mask, float('-inf'))
        att = F.softmax(att, dim=-1)
        att = self.drop(att)
        
        # Apply attention to values
        y = (att @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, C)
        return self.proj(y)

Notice how every component maps directly to what we built in NumPy. The architecture is identical — the difference is that PyTorch tracks the computation graph and can compute gradients through every single operation.

Part 5: The PyTorch Training Loop

Now for the training loop. This is where the magic happens — where PyTorch’s autograd enables learning that NumPy cannot achieve.

The AdamW Optimizer

We use AdamW instead of basic SGD (Stochastic Gradient Descent). AdamW is the standard optimizer for training Transformers because it:

  • Adapts learning rates per parameter — parameters that need bigger updates get them, others get smaller updates
  • Uses momentum — smooths out noisy gradients by averaging over recent steps
  • Decouples weight decay — regularization is applied correctly, preventing overfitting

Cosine Learning Rate Schedule with Warmup

The learning rate is not constant during training. We use a cosine schedule with warmup:

  1. Warmup phase (first ~10% of steps): learning rate increases linearly from 0 to the peak value. This prevents the model from making wild updates before it has seen enough data.
  2. Cosine decay phase (remaining 90%): learning rate smoothly decreases following a cosine curve, settling near zero. This allows fine-grained refinement in later training.

Gradient Clipping

Sometimes gradients can “explode” — become extremely large due to certain input patterns. Gradient clipping caps the gradient magnitude to prevent this:

torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)

This says: if the total gradient norm exceeds 1.0, scale all gradients down proportionally. It is a safety net that prevents training from diverging.

Part 6: What Changes vs NumPy

Let us be precise about what PyTorch training achieves that NumPy cannot:

ALL Parameters Now Receive Gradient Updates

ComponentNumPy (Updated?)PyTorch (Updated?)Impact
Token EmbeddingsYesYesLearns word meanings
Position EmbeddingsNoYesLearns position-aware patterns
Q, K, V ProjectionsNoYesLearns what to attend to
Output ProjectionNoYesLearns how to combine attention
FFN Layer 1NoYesLearns feature extraction
FFN Layer 2NoYesLearns feature combination
Layer Norm (gamma, beta)NoYesLearns distribution normalization
Output HeadYesYes (tied)Learns token prediction

With NumPy, only 2 out of 8 component types get updated. With PyTorch, all 8 component types receive meaningful gradient updates. That is the difference between a model that barely beats random and one that genuinely learns language.

What Each Component Learns

  • Attention weights learn to attend to relevant tokens: The Q, K, V projections learn which words are relevant to each other. After training, a verb might attend strongly to its subject, an adjective to its noun.
  • FFN weights learn to store and process patterns: Research suggests the feed-forward layers act as “memory banks,” storing factual knowledge and common patterns.
  • Layer norms learn to stabilize distributions: Each layer norm learns the optimal scale and shift for its position in the network, keeping activations in a healthy range.
  • Position embeddings learn sequential patterns: The model learns that position 0 often starts sentences, certain positions are common for verbs vs nouns, and so on.

Part 7: GPU vs CPU Training

PyTorch can run on either CPU (your regular processor) or GPU (your graphics card). Here is what you need to know:

FactorCPUGPU (CUDA)
Works onEvery computerRequires NVIDIA GPU
Speed (small model)Adequate5–20x faster
Speed (large model)Very slow50–100x faster
MemorySystem RAM (8–64 GB)GPU VRAM (4–24 GB typically)
SetupNo extra setupNeed CUDA drivers + GPU PyTorch

For our NeuralForge models (1M – 10M parameters), CPU training is perfectly fine. You can train on Tiny Shakespeare in minutes on a modern laptop. GPU becomes necessary only when scaling to larger models or datasets.

To use GPU in PyTorch when available:

device = 'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'
model = MiniGPT2Torch(...).to(device)
# When creating tensors for training:
inputs = inputs.to(device)
targets = targets.to(device)

Part 8: Putting It All Together

The complete training function combines everything: model creation, optimizer setup, learning rate scheduling, the training loop, and evaluation:

def pretrain_torch(text, vocab_size=4096, d_model=128, n_heads=4, 
                   n_layers=4, max_seq_len=128, n_steps=30, 
                   batch_size=8, lr=3e-4):
    """Train a PyTorch GPT-2 model from scratch."""
    
    device = 'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'
    print(f"Training on: {device}")
    
    # Create model
    model = MiniGPT2Torch(
        vocab_size=vocab_size,
        d_model=d_model,
        n_heads=n_heads,
        n_layers=n_layers,
        max_seq_len=max_seq_len
    ).to(device)
    
    n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
    print(f"Model parameters: {n_params:,}")
    
    # Optimizer: AdamW with weight decay
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(
        model.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=0.01
    )
    
    # Training loop
    model.train()
    for step in range(n_steps):
        # Get batch (simplified: random sequences from tokenized text)
        batch = get_batch(text, batch_size, max_seq_len, vocab_size, device)
        inputs, targets = batch
        
        # Forward pass
        logits, loss = model(inputs, targets)
        
        # Backward pass: compute ALL gradients
        loss.backward()
        
        # Gradient clipping
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
        
        # Update ALL parameters
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        
        if step % 5 == 0:
            print(f"Step {step:3d} | Loss: {loss.item():.4f}")
    
    return model

That is the complete training pipeline. Three lines do the critical work: loss.backward() computes all gradients, optimizer.step() updates all parameters, and optimizer.zero_grad() resets for the next step.

Part 9: Comparing NumPy vs PyTorch Results

The difference is dramatic. Here is what you can expect when training the same architecture on Tiny Shakespeare:

In 30 steps with PyTorch, the model learns more than in 500 steps with NumPy. That is the power of training all parameters simultaneously.

Why NumPy Training Still Matters: You might wonder: if PyTorch is so much better, why did we spend lectures building in NumPy? Because understanding comes from building. You now know what every matrix multiplication does, what every component computes, and why the architecture is designed this way. PyTorch is a tool that automates the calculus — but you understand the machine it is computing on.

Summary

In this lecture, you learned:

  • The NumPy limitation: Our manual training only updates ~8% of parameters, achieving just 9.9% loss improvement
  • What PyTorch is: A deep learning framework with automatic gradient computation (autograd)
  • How autograd works: Forward pass builds a computation graph, backward() traverses it to compute all gradients
  • The PyTorch model: Same architecture as NumPy, using nn.Module, nn.Linear, nn.Embedding, nn.LayerNorm
  • Weight tying: Output head shares weights with token embedding for efficiency
  • The training loop: AdamW optimizer, cosine LR schedule, gradient clipping
  • What changes: ALL parameters now receive gradient updates — attention, FFN, layer norms, positions
  • The result: 55.9% loss improvement in 30 steps vs 9.9% in 500 steps
  • GPU vs CPU: CPU is fine for small models; GPU needed for larger-scale training

In the next lecture, we will take this trained model and fine-tune it — adapting it to specific tasks using LoRA, the technique that makes fine-tuning efficient even on consumer hardware.

Introducere: Problema NumPy

În lecțiile anterioare, am construit un model GPT-2 complet în NumPy. Am implementat forward pass-uri, am calculat cross-entropy loss și am scris chiar și o buclă de antrenament. Dar exista o limitare fundamentală: train_step-ul nostru NumPy actualizează doar aproximativ 8% din parametrii modelului — mai exact, output head-ul și token embeddings.

De ce? Pentru că, pentru a calcula gradienții pentru fiecare parametru prin întregul Transformer — prin straturile de attention, rețelele feed-forward, layer norms și conexiunile reziduale — trebuie să implementezi backpropagation manual pentru fiecare operație. Aceasta înseamnă sute de calcule de derivate, fiecare dintre ele o potențială sursă de erori.

Rezultatul? Antrenamentul nostru NumPy abia învață:

Loss Inițial3.743.46
Loss Final (după antrenament)3.37 (500 pași)1.53 (30 pași)
Reducerea Loss-ului9,9%55,9%
Referință Aleatorie3.71 (loss-ul când ghicești aleatoriu dintre ~4096 tokens)
Parametri Actualizați~8% (head + embeddings)100% (toți parametrii)
Viteză de Antrenament~1 pas/sec~10+ pași/sec (CPU), ~100+ (GPU)

Privește aceste numere cu atenție. După 500 de pași de antrenament, modelul nostru NumPy abia depășește referința aleatorie (3.37 vs 3.71). Între timp, PyTorch atinge 1.53 în doar 30 de pași — aceasta este învățare reală. Modelul începe să prezică următorul token cu o înțelegere reală, nu doar zgomot statistic.

De Ce Contează: Un loss de 3.37 înseamnă că modelul tău în esență ghicește. Un loss de 1.53 înseamnă că a învățat tipare semnificative — poate completa propoziții, poate urma reguli gramaticale și poate genera text recognoscibil. Aceasta este diferența dintre o demonstrație simplă și un model de limbaj real.

Partea 1: Ce este PyTorch?

PyTorch este un framework de deep learning creat de Meta (Facebook) care face un lucru esențial pe care codul nostru NumPy nu îl poate face: calculează automat gradienții pentru fiecare parametru din modelul tău.

Gândește-te astfel:

  • NumPy este un calculator — face matematica pe care i-o spui să o facă, nimic mai mult
  • PyTorch este un calculator care își amintește și fiecare calcul efectuat, astfel încât poate trasa înapoi și determina cum a influențat fiecare intrare rezultatul

Această „memorare" se numește autograd (calculul automat al gradienților) și este ceea ce face antrenamentul rețelelor neuronale adânci practic posibil.

Instalarea PyTorch

PyTorch se instalează cu pip, la fel ca orice alt pachet Python:

pip install torch
Avertisment privind Dimensiunea: PyTorch este un pachet mare — aproximativ 500 MB până la 2 GB, în funcție de platformă și de dacă instalezi suport GPU. Versiunea doar pentru CPU este mai mică. Dacă ai o conexiune lentă, ai răbdare în timpul descărcării. Vestea bună: îl instalezi o singură dată.

Pentru a verifica instalarea:

import torch
print(f"PyTorch version: {torch.__version__}")
print(f"CUDA available: {torch.cuda.is_available()}")

Partea 2: Cum Funcționează Autograd

Acesta este cel mai important concept din această lecție. Nu te îngrijora de matematică — concentrează-te pe intuiție.

Forward Pass: Construirea unui Graf de Calcul

Când efectuezi calcule cu tensori PyTorch, PyTorch construiește în secret un graf de calcul — o înregistrare a fiecărei operații efectuate. Imaginează-ți că calculezi:

x = torch.tensor([2.0], requires_grad=True)
y = x * 3      # PyTorch records: "y = x * 3"
z = y + 1      # PyTorch records: "z = y + 1"
loss = z ** 2  # PyTorch records: "loss = z ** 2"

După acest forward pass, PyTorch are un graf intern:

x (2.0) → [multiply by 3] → y (6.0) → [add 1] → z (7.0) → [square] → loss (49.0)

Backward Pass: Calcularea Tuturor Gradienților

Când apelezi loss.backward(), PyTorch parcurge acest graf în sens invers, folosind regula lanțului din calcul diferențial pentru a determina cât de mult a contribuit fiecare parametru la loss:

loss.backward()
print(x.grad)  # tensor([42.0])

PyTorch a calculat: d(loss)/dx = d(z²)/dz × dz/dy × dy/dx = 2z × 1 × 3 = 2(7) × 3 = 42.

Nu a trebuit să derivezi acea formulă. PyTorch a făcut-o automat. Acum scalează asta la un model cu milioane de parametri și sute de operații — PyTorch calculează toți gradienții într-un singur apel backward().

Ideea Cheie: În modelul nostru NumPy, am calculat manual gradienții pentru output head și embeddings. Nu am putut calcula gradienții pentru ponderile de attention, straturile FFN sau layer norms fără a scrie sute de linii de cod pentru derivate. Autograd-ul PyTorch gestionează toate acestea automat, ceea ce înseamnă că fiecare parametru este actualizat în timpul antrenamentului.

Pasul Optimizatorului: Actualizarea Parametrilor

Odată ce gradienții sunt calculați, optimizatorul îi folosește pentru a actualiza fiecare parametru:

# After loss.backward() computes all gradients:
optimizer.step()  # Update every parameter: param = param - lr * param.grad
optimizer.zero_grad()  # Reset gradients for the next step

Acest dans în trei pași — forward, backward, step — este bătaia inimii întregului antrenament de deep learning.

Partea 3: Conversia Modelului Nostru în PyTorch

Modelul nostru PyTorch are exact aceeași arhitectură ca modelul nostru NumPy. Același număr de straturi, același mecanism de attention, aceeași rețea feed-forward. Singura diferență este framework-ul de implementare — care permite calculul complet al gradienților.

Patternul nn.Module

Fiecare model PyTorch moștenește din nn.Module. Aceasta îi oferă capacitatea de a:

  • Urmări automat toți parametrii (ponderi și bias-uri)
  • Muta pe GPU cu un singur apel .to('cuda')
  • Salva și încărca cu torch.save() și torch.load()
  • Comuta între modurile de antrenament și evaluare

Weight Tying

O optimizare importantă în modelele de limbaj moderne: output head-ul partajează ponderile cu token embedding. Aceasta se numește weight tying.

De ce are sens? Token embedding-ul convertește ID-urile de token în vectori. Output head-ul convertește vectorii înapoi în probabilități de token. Acestea sunt operații inverse — astfel că partajarea aceleiași matrice de ponderi face modelul să învețe o reprezentare mai consistentă.

# In practice, weight tying looks like this:
self.token_embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)
# ... later, in the forward pass:
logits = x @ self.token_embedding.weight.T  # Reuse embedding weights as output head

Aceasta reduce și numărul total de parametri — matricea de embedding este adesea cea mai mare matrice de ponderi din model.

Partea 4: Modelul PyTorch Complet

Clasa de model de mai jos este o traducere directă a GPT-2 nostru din NumPy în PyTorch. Fiecare componentă corespunde unu-la-unu:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import math

class MiniGPT2Torch(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, d_model, n_heads, n_layers, max_seq_len, d_ff=None):
        super().__init__()
        self.d_model = d_model
        self.n_heads = n_heads
        self.n_layers = n_layers
        self.head_dim = d_model // n_heads
        d_ff = d_ff or 4 * d_model

        # Token and position embeddings
        self.token_embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)
        self.position_embedding = nn.Embedding(max_seq_len, d_model)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(0.1)

        # Transformer layers
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([
            TransformerBlock(d_model, n_heads, d_ff)
            for _ in range(n_layers)
        ])

        # Final layer norm
        self.ln_f = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)

        # Weight tying: output head reuses token embedding
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(d_model, vocab_size, bias=False)
        self.lm_head.weight = self.token_embedding.weight

        # Initialize weights
        self.apply(self._init_weights)

    def _init_weights(self, module):
        if isinstance(module, nn.Linear):
            torch.nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.02)
            if module.bias is not None:
                torch.nn.init.zeros_(module.bias)
        elif isinstance(module, nn.Embedding):
            torch.nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.02)

    def forward(self, idx, targets=None):
        B, T = idx.shape

        # Embeddings
        tok_emb = self.token_embedding(idx)
        pos_emb = self.position_embedding(torch.arange(T, device=idx.device))
        x = self.drop(tok_emb + pos_emb)

        # Transformer layers
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x)

        x = self.ln_f(x)
        logits = self.lm_head(x)

        # Compute loss if targets provided
        loss = None
        if targets is not None:
            loss = F.cross_entropy(
                logits.view(-1, logits.size(-1)),
                targets.view(-1)
            )

        return logits, loss

Și blocul Transformer:

class TransformerBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, d_ff):
        super().__init__()
        self.ln1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.attn = CausalSelfAttention(d_model, n_heads)
        self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.ffn = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff),
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model),
            nn.Dropout(0.1),
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.attn(self.ln1(x))   # Residual + attention
        x = x + self.ffn(self.ln2(x))    # Residual + FFN
        return x


class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads):
        super().__init__()
        self.n_heads = n_heads
        self.head_dim = d_model // n_heads

        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model)
        self.proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(0.1)

    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape

        # Compute Q, K, V in one matrix multiply
        qkv = self.qkv(x).reshape(B, T, 3, self.n_heads, self.head_dim)
        q, k, v = qkv.permute(2, 0, 3, 1, 4)  # 3 x (B, heads, T, head_dim)

        # Scaled dot-product attention with causal mask
        att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(self.head_dim)
        mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, device=x.device), diagonal=1).bool()
        att = att.masked_fill(mask, float('-inf'))
        att = F.softmax(att, dim=-1)
        att = self.drop(att)

        # Apply attention to values
        y = (att @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, C)
        return self.proj(y)

Observă cum fiecare componentă corespunde direct cu ceea ce am construit în NumPy. Arhitectura este identică — diferența este că PyTorch urmărește graful de calcul și poate calcula gradienții prin fiecare operație.

Partea 5: Bucla de Antrenament PyTorch

Acum vine bucla de antrenament. Aici se întâmplă magia — unde autograd-ul PyTorch permite o învățare pe care NumPy nu o poate realiza.

Optimizatorul AdamW

Folosim AdamW în loc de SGD (Stochastic Gradient Descent) de bază. AdamW este optimizatorul standard pentru antrenamentul Transformers deoarece:

  • Adaptează ratele de învățare per parametru — parametrii care au nevoie de actualizări mai mari le primesc, ceilalți primesc actualizări mai mici
  • Folosește momentum — netezește gradienții zgomotoși prin medierea pe pașii recenți
  • Decuplează weight decay — regularizarea este aplicată corect, prevenind overfitting-ul

Programul de Learning Rate Cosinus cu Warmup

Rata de învățare nu este constantă în timpul antrenamentului. Folosim un program cosinus cu warmup:

  1. Faza de warmup (primii ~10% din pași): rata de învățare crește liniar de la 0 la valoarea maximă. Aceasta previne actualizări haotice ale modelului înainte de a fi văzut suficiente date.
  2. Faza de descreștere cosinus (restul de 90%): rata de învățare scade lin urmând o curbă cosinus, stabilizându-se aproape de zero. Aceasta permite rafinare de precizie în fazele ulterioare ale antrenamentului.

Gradient Clipping

Uneori gradienții pot „exploda" — devin extrem de mari din cauza anumitor tipare de intrare. Gradient clipping limitează magnitudinea gradientului pentru a preveni aceasta:

torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)

Aceasta spune: dacă norma totală a gradientului depășește 1.0, redu proporțional toți gradienții. Este o plasă de siguranță care previne divergența antrenamentului.

Partea 6: Ce Se Schimbă față de NumPy

Să fim preciși despre ce realizează antrenamentul PyTorch față de ceea ce NumPy nu poate:

Cu NumPy, doar 2 din 8 tipuri de componente sunt actualizate. Cu PyTorch, toate cele 8 tipuri de componente primesc actualizări semnificative de gradient. Aceasta este diferența dintre un model care abia depășește aleatoriul și unul care învață cu adevărat limbajul.

Ce Învață Fiecare Componentă

  • Ponderile de attention învață să acorde atenție token-urilor relevante: Proiecțiile Q, K, V învață care cuvinte sunt relevante unele pentru altele. După antrenament, un verb ar putea acorda atenție puternică subiectului său, un adjectiv substantivului său.
  • Ponderile FFN învață să stocheze și să proceseze tipare: Cercetările sugerează că straturile feed-forward acționează ca „bănci de memorie", stocând cunoștințe factuale și tipare comune.
  • Layer norms învață să stabilizeze distribuțiile: Fiecare layer norm învață scala și deplasarea optimă pentru poziția sa în rețea, menținând activările într-un interval sănătos.
  • Position embeddings învață tipare secvențiale: Modelul învață că poziția 0 începe adesea propozițiile, anumite poziții sunt comune pentru verbe vs substantive și așa mai departe.

Partea 7: Antrenament GPU vs CPU

PyTorch poate rula fie pe CPU (procesorul tău obișnuit), fie pe GPU (placa ta grafică). Iată ce trebuie să știi:

Pentru a folosi GPU în PyTorch când este disponibil:

Partea 8: Punând Totul Cap la Cap

Funcția completă de antrenament combină totul: crearea modelului, configurarea optimizatorului, programarea ratei de învățare, bucla de antrenament și evaluarea:

def pretrain_torch(text, vocab_size=4096, d_model=128, n_heads=4,
                   n_layers=4, max_seq_len=128, n_steps=30,
                   batch_size=8, lr=3e-4):
    """Train a PyTorch GPT-2 model from scratch."""

    device = 'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'
    print(f"Training on: {device}")

    # Create model
    model = MiniGPT2Torch(
        vocab_size=vocab_size,
        d_model=d_model,
        n_heads=n_heads,
        n_layers=n_layers,
        max_seq_len=max_seq_len
    ).to(device)

    n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
    print(f"Model parameters: {n_params:,}")

    # Optimizer: AdamW with weight decay
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(
        model.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=0.01
    )

    # Training loop
    model.train()
    for step in range(n_steps):
        # Get batch (simplified: random sequences from tokenized text)
        batch = get_batch(text, batch_size, max_seq_len, vocab_size, device)
        inputs, targets = batch

        # Forward pass
        logits, loss = model(inputs, targets)

        # Backward pass: compute ALL gradients
        loss.backward()

        # Gradient clipping
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)

        # Update ALL parameters
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()

        if step % 5 == 0:
            print(f"Step {step:3d} | Loss: {loss.item():.4f}")

    return model

Aceasta este întreaga conductă de antrenament. Trei linii fac munca esențială: loss.backward() calculează toți gradienții, optimizer.step() actualizează toți parametrii, iar optimizer.zero_grad() resetează pentru pasul următor.

Diferența este dramatică. Iată la ce te poți aștepta când antrenezi aceeași arhitectură pe Tiny Shakespeare:

În 30 de pași cu PyTorch, modelul învață mai mult decât în 500 de pași cu NumPy. Aceasta este puterea antrenării tuturor parametrilor simultan.

De Ce Contează Totuși Antrenamentul NumPy: Te-ai putea întreba: dacă PyTorch este atât de mult mai bun, de ce am petrecut lecții construind în NumPy? Pentru că înțelegerea vine din construire. Acum știi ce face fiecare înmulțire de matrice, ce calculează fiecare componentă și de ce este arhitectura proiectată astfel. PyTorch este un instrument care automatizează calculul diferențial — dar tu înțelegi mașina pe care o calculează.

Rezumat

În această lecție, ai învățat:

  • Limitarea NumPy: Antrenamentul nostru manual actualizează doar ~8% din parametri, obținând doar 9,9% îmbunătățire a loss-ului
  • Ce este PyTorch: Un framework de deep learning cu calcul automat al gradienților (autograd)
  • Cum funcționează autograd: Forward pass-ul construiește un graf de calcul, backward() îl parcurge pentru a calcula toți gradienții
  • Modelul PyTorch: Aceeași arhitectură ca NumPy, folosind nn.Module, nn.Linear, nn.Embedding, nn.LayerNorm
  • Weight tying: Output head-ul partajează ponderile cu token embedding pentru eficiență
  • Bucla de antrenament: Optimizator AdamW, program de LR cosinus, gradient clipping
  • Ce se schimbă: TOȚI parametrii primesc acum actualizări de gradient — attention, FFN, layer norms, positions
  • Rezultatul: 55,9% îmbunătățire a loss-ului în 30 de pași vs 9,9% în 500 de pași
  • GPU vs CPU: CPU este suficient pentru modele mici; GPU necesar pentru antrenament la scară mai mare

Μέρος 1: Τι Είναι το PyTorch;

Το PyTorch είναι ένα framework deep learning που δημιουργήθηκε από τη Meta (Facebook) και κάνει ένα κρίσιμο πράγμα που ο κώδικας NumPy μας δεν μπορεί: υπολογίζει αυτόματα τα gradients για κάθε παράμετρο του μοντέλου σας.

Σκεφτείτε το ως εξής:

  • Το NumPy είναι ένα κομπιουτεράκι — κάνει τα μαθηματικά που του λέτε, τίποτα παραπάνω
  • Το PyTorch είναι ένα κομπιουτεράκι που θυμάται και κάθε υπολογισμό που εκτέλεσε, ώστε να μπορεί να ανιχνεύσει πώς κάθε είσοδος επηρέασε το αποτέλεσμα

Αυτή η «απομνημόνευση» ονομάζεται autograd (αυτόματος υπολογισμός gradients) και είναι αυτό που καθιστά πρακτική την εκπαίδευση βαθιών νευρωνικών δικτύων.

Εγκατάσταση του PyTorch

Το PyTorch εγκαθίσταται με pip, όπως κάθε άλλο πακέτο Python:

pip install torch
Προειδοποίηση Μεγέθους: Το PyTorch είναι ένα μεγάλο πακέτο — περίπου 500 MB έως 2 GB ανάλογα με την πλατφόρμα σας και αν εγκαταστήσετε υποστήριξη GPU. Η έκδοση μόνο για CPU είναι μικρότερη. Αν έχετε αργή σύνδεση, κάντε υπομονή κατά τη λήψη. Τα καλά νέα: το εγκαθιστάτε μόνο μία φορά.

Για να επαληθεύσετε την εγκατάσταση:

import torch
print(f"PyTorch version: {torch.__version__}")
print(f"CUDA available: {torch.cuda.is_available()}")

Μέρος 2: Πώς Λειτουργεί το Autograd

Αυτή είναι η πιο σημαντική έννοια σε αυτό το μάθημα. Μην ανησυχείτε για τα μαθηματικά — εστιάστε στη διαίσθηση.

Το Forward Pass: Κατασκευή ενός Γράφου Υπολογισμού

Όταν εκτελείτε υπολογισμούς με tensors του PyTorch, το PyTorch κατασκευάζει κρυφά ένα γράφο υπολογισμού — μια καταγραφή κάθε πράξης που εκτελέστηκε. Φανταστείτε ότι υπολογίζετε:

x = torch.tensor([2.0], requires_grad=True)
y = x * 3      # PyTorch records: "y = x * 3"
z = y + 1      # PyTorch records: "z = y + 1"
loss = z ** 2  # PyTorch records: "loss = z ** 2"

Μετά από αυτό το forward pass, το PyTorch έχει έναν εσωτερικό γράφο:

x (2.0) → [multiply by 3] → y (6.0) → [add 1] → z (7.0) → [square] → loss (49.0)

Το Backward Pass: Υπολογισμός Όλων των Gradients

Όταν καλείτε loss.backward(), το PyTorch διασχίζει αυτόν τον γράφο αντίστροφα, χρησιμοποιώντας τον κανόνα της αλυσίδας του διαφορικού λογισμού για να υπολογίσει πόσο συνέβαλε κάθε παράμετρος στο loss:

loss.backward()
print(x.grad)  # tensor([42.0])

Το PyTorch υπολόγισε: d(loss)/dx = d(z²)/dz × dz/dy × dy/dx = 2z × 1 × 3 = 2(7) × 3 = 42.

Δεν χρειάστηκε να παραγωγίσετε εκείνο τον τύπο. Το PyTorch το έκανε αυτόματα. Τώρα κλιμακώστε αυτό σε ένα μοντέλο με εκατομμύρια παραμέτρους και εκατοντάδες πράξεις — το PyTorch υπολογίζει όλα τα gradients σε μία κλήση backward().

Η Βασική Ιδέα: Στο μοντέλο NumPy μας, υπολογίσαμε χειροκίνητα τα gradients για το output head και τα embeddings. Δεν μπορούσαμε να υπολογίσουμε τα gradients για τα βάρη attention, τα επίπεδα FFN ή τα layer norms χωρίς να γράψουμε εκατοντάδες γραμμές κώδικα παραγώγων. Το autograd του PyTorch χειρίζεται όλα αυτά αυτόματα, που σημαίνει ότι κάθε παράμετρος ενημερώνεται κατά την εκπαίδευση.

Το Βήμα του Optimizer: Ενημέρωση Παραμέτρων

Μόλις υπολογιστούν τα gradients, ο optimizer τα χρησιμοποιεί για να ενημερώσει κάθε παράμετρο:

# After loss.backward() computes all gradients:
optimizer.step()  # Update every parameter: param = param - lr * param.grad
optimizer.zero_grad()  # Reset gradients for the next step

Αυτός ο χορός τριών βημάτων — forward, backward, step — είναι ο παλμός κάθε εκπαίδευσης deep learning.

Μέρος 3: Μετατροπή του Μοντέλου μας σε PyTorch

Το μοντέλο PyTorch μας έχει ακριβώς την ίδια αρχιτεκτονική με το μοντέλο NumPy μας. Ίδιος αριθμός επιπέδων, ίδιος μηχανισμός attention, ίδιο δίκτυο feed-forward. Η μόνη διαφορά είναι το framework υλοποίησης — που επιτρέπει τον πλήρη υπολογισμό gradients.

Το Μοτίβο nn.Module

Κάθε μοντέλο PyTorch κληρονομεί από nn.Module. Αυτό του δίνει τη δυνατότητα να:

  • Παρακολουθεί αυτόματα όλες τις παραμέτρους (βάρη και biases)
  • Μεταφέρεται σε GPU με μία κλήση .to('cuda')
  • Αποθηκεύεται και φορτώνεται με torch.save() και torch.load()
  • Εναλλάσσεται μεταξύ λειτουργίας εκπαίδευσης και αξιολόγησης

Weight Tying

Μια σημαντική βελτιστοποίηση στα σύγχρονα γλωσσικά μοντέλα: το output head μοιράζεται βάρη με το token embedding. Αυτό ονομάζεται weight tying.

Γιατί είναι λογικό; Το token embedding μετατρέπει τα token IDs σε διανύσματα. Το output head μετατρέπει τα διανύσματα πίσω σε πιθανότητες token. Αυτές είναι αντίστροφες πράξεις — επομένως η κοινή χρήση του ίδιου πίνακα βαρών κάνει το μοντέλο να μαθαίνει μια πιο συνεπή αναπαράσταση.

# In practice, weight tying looks like this:
self.token_embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)
# ... later, in the forward pass:
logits = x @ self.token_embedding.weight.T  # Reuse embedding weights as output head

Αυτό μειώνει επίσης τον συνολικό αριθμό παραμέτρων — ο πίνακας embedding είναι συχνά ο μεγαλύτερος πίνακας βαρών στο μοντέλο.

Μέρος 4: Το Πλήρες Μοντέλο PyTorch

Η κλάση μοντέλου παρακάτω είναι μια άμεση μεταφορά του GPT-2 μας από NumPy σε PyTorch. Κάθε στοιχείο αντιστοιχεί ένα-προς-ένα:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import math

class MiniGPT2Torch(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, d_model, n_heads, n_layers, max_seq_len, d_ff=None):
        super().__init__()
        self.d_model = d_model
        self.n_heads = n_heads
        self.n_layers = n_layers
        self.head_dim = d_model // n_heads
        d_ff = d_ff or 4 * d_model

        # Token and position embeddings
        self.token_embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)
        self.position_embedding = nn.Embedding(max_seq_len, d_model)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(0.1)

        # Transformer layers
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([
            TransformerBlock(d_model, n_heads, d_ff)
            for _ in range(n_layers)
        ])

        # Final layer norm
        self.ln_f = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)

        # Weight tying: output head reuses token embedding
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(d_model, vocab_size, bias=False)
        self.lm_head.weight = self.token_embedding.weight

        # Initialize weights
        self.apply(self._init_weights)

    def _init_weights(self, module):
        if isinstance(module, nn.Linear):
            torch.nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.02)
            if module.bias is not None:
                torch.nn.init.zeros_(module.bias)
        elif isinstance(module, nn.Embedding):
            torch.nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.02)

    def forward(self, idx, targets=None):
        B, T = idx.shape

        # Embeddings
        tok_emb = self.token_embedding(idx)
        pos_emb = self.position_embedding(torch.arange(T, device=idx.device))
        x = self.drop(tok_emb + pos_emb)

        # Transformer layers
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x)

        x = self.ln_f(x)
        logits = self.lm_head(x)

        # Compute loss if targets provided
        loss = None
        if targets is not None:
            loss = F.cross_entropy(
                logits.view(-1, logits.size(-1)),
                targets.view(-1)
            )

        return logits, loss

Και το Transformer block:

class TransformerBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, d_ff):
        super().__init__()
        self.ln1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.attn = CausalSelfAttention(d_model, n_heads)
        self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.ffn = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff),
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model),
            nn.Dropout(0.1),
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + self.attn(self.ln1(x))   # Residual + attention
        x = x + self.ffn(self.ln2(x))    # Residual + FFN
        return x


class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads):
        super().__init__()
        self.n_heads = n_heads
        self.head_dim = d_model // n_heads

        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model)
        self.proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(0.1)

    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape

        # Compute Q, K, V in one matrix multiply
        qkv = self.qkv(x).reshape(B, T, 3, self.n_heads, self.head_dim)
        q, k, v = qkv.permute(2, 0, 3, 1, 4)  # 3 x (B, heads, T, head_dim)

        # Scaled dot-product attention with causal mask
        att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(self.head_dim)
        mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, device=x.device), diagonal=1).bool()
        att = att.masked_fill(mask, float('-inf'))
        att = F.softmax(att, dim=-1)
        att = self.drop(att)

        # Apply attention to values
        y = (att @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, C)
        return self.proj(y)

Παρατηρήστε πώς κάθε στοιχείο αντιστοιχεί άμεσα σε αυτό που χτίσαμε σε NumPy. Η αρχιτεκτονική είναι πανομοιότυπη — η διαφορά είναι ότι το PyTorch παρακολουθεί τον γράφο υπολογισμού και μπορεί να υπολογίσει gradients μέσα από κάθε πράξη.

Μέρος 5: Ο Βρόχος Εκπαίδευσης PyTorch

Τώρα ο βρόχος εκπαίδευσης. Εδώ γίνεται η μαγεία — όπου το autograd του PyTorch επιτρέπει μάθηση που το NumPy δεν μπορεί να επιτύχει.

Ο Optimizer AdamW

Χρησιμοποιούμε AdamW αντί για βασικό SGD (Stochastic Gradient Descent). Ο AdamW είναι ο τυπικός optimizer για εκπαίδευση Transformers επειδή:

  • Προσαρμόζει τα learning rates ανά παράμετρο — παράμετροι που χρειάζονται μεγαλύτερες ενημερώσεις τις λαμβάνουν, οι υπόλοιπες λαμβάνουν μικρότερες
  • Χρησιμοποιεί momentum — εξομαλύνει τα θορυβώδη gradients μέσω μέσου όρου πρόσφατων βημάτων
  • Αποσυνδέει το weight decay — η regularization εφαρμόζεται σωστά, αποτρέποντας το overfitting

Πρόγραμμα Learning Rate Cosine με Warmup

Το learning rate δεν είναι σταθερό κατά τη διάρκεια της εκπαίδευσης. Χρησιμοποιούμε ένα πρόγραμμα cosine με warmup:

  1. Φάση warmup (πρώτο ~10% των βημάτων): το learning rate αυξάνεται γραμμικά από 0 στην κορυφαία τιμή. Αυτό αποτρέπει το μοντέλο από χαοτικές ενημερώσεις πριν δει αρκετά δεδομένα.
  2. Φάση μείωσης cosine (υπόλοιπο 90%): το learning rate μειώνεται ομαλά ακολουθώντας μια καμπύλη cosine, σταθεροποιούμενο κοντά στο μηδέν. Αυτό επιτρέπει λεπτομερή βελτιστοποίηση στα μεταγενέστερα στάδια εκπαίδευσης.

Gradient Clipping

Μερικές φορές τα gradients μπορεί να «εκραγούν» — να γίνουν εξαιρετικά μεγάλα λόγω ορισμένων μοτίβων εισόδου. Το gradient clipping περιορίζει το μέγεθος του gradient για να το αποτρέψει:

torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)

Αυτό λέει: αν η συνολική νόρμα του gradient υπερβαίνει το 1.0, κλιμάκωσε αναλογικά όλα τα gradients. Είναι ένα δίχτυ ασφαλείας που αποτρέπει την απόκλιση της εκπαίδευσης.

Μέρος 6: Τι Αλλάζει σε Σχέση με το NumPy

Ας είμαστε ακριβείς σχετικά με το τι επιτυγχάνει η εκπαίδευση PyTorch που το NumPy δεν μπορεί:

ΟΛΕΣ οι Παράμετροι Λαμβάνουν Τώρα Ενημερώσεις Gradient

ΣτοιχείοNumPy (Ενημερώνεται;)PyTorch (Ενημερώνεται;)Επίδραση
Token EmbeddingsΝαιΝαιΜαθαίνει τις σημασίες λέξεων
Position EmbeddingsΌχιΝαιΜαθαίνει μοτίβα βασισμένα σε θέση
Προβολές Q, K, VΌχιΝαιΜαθαίνει σε τι να δίνει προσοχή
Προβολή ΕξόδουΌχιΝαιΜαθαίνει πώς να συνδυάζει attention
FFN Επίπεδο 1ΌχιΝαιΜαθαίνει εξαγωγή χαρακτηριστικών
FFN Επίπεδο 2ΌχιΝαιΜαθαίνει συνδυασμό χαρακτηριστικών

Με NumPy, μόνο 2 από 8 τύποι στοιχείων ενημερώνονται. Με PyTorch, και οι 8 τύποι στοιχείων λαμβάνουν ουσιαστικές ενημερώσεις gradient. Αυτή είναι η διαφορά μεταξύ ενός μοντέλου που μόλις ξεπερνά το τυχαίο και ενός που πραγματικά μαθαίνει γλώσσα.

Τι Μαθαίνει Κάθε Στοιχείο

  • Τα βάρη attention μαθαίνουν να δίνουν προσοχή σε σχετικά tokens: Οι προβολές Q, K, V μαθαίνουν ποιες λέξεις είναι σχετικές μεταξύ τους. Μετά την εκπαίδευση, ένα ρήμα μπορεί να δίνει μεγάλη προσοχή στο υποκείμενό του, ένα επίθετο στο ουσιαστικό του.
  • Τα βάρη FFN μαθαίνουν να αποθηκεύουν και να επεξεργάζονται μοτίβα: Η έρευνα υποδεικνύει ότι τα επίπεδα feed-forward λειτουργούν ως «τράπεζες μνήμης», αποθηκεύοντας πραγματική γνώση και κοινά μοτίβα.
  • Τα layer norms μαθαίνουν να σταθεροποιούν τις κατανομές: Κάθε layer norm μαθαίνει τη βέλτιστη κλίμακα και μετατόπιση για τη θέση του στο δίκτυο, διατηρώντας τις ενεργοποιήσεις σε υγιές εύρος.
  • Τα position embeddings μαθαίνουν ακολουθιακά μοτίβα: Το μοντέλο μαθαίνει ότι η θέση 0 συχνά ξεκινά προτάσεις, ορισμένες θέσεις είναι συνηθισμένες για ρήματα έναντι ουσιαστικών, και ούτω καθεξής.

Μέρος 7: Εκπαίδευση GPU έναντι CPU

Το PyTorch μπορεί να εκτελεστεί είτε σε CPU (τον κανονικό σας επεξεργαστή) είτε σε GPU (την κάρτα γραφικών σας). Να τι πρέπει να γνωρίζετε:

Για τα μοντέλα NeuralForge μας (1M – 10M παράμετροι), η εκπαίδευση σε CPU είναι απόλυτα επαρκής. Μπορείτε να εκπαιδεύσετε στο Tiny Shakespeare σε λίγα λεπτά σε ένα σύγχρονο laptop. Η GPU γίνεται απαραίτητη μόνο όταν κλιμακώνετε σε μεγαλύτερα μοντέλα ή σύνολα δεδομένων.

Για χρήση GPU στο PyTorch όταν είναι διαθέσιμη:

Μέρος 8: Βάζοντας τα Όλα Μαζί

Η πλήρης συνάρτηση εκπαίδευσης συνδυάζει τα πάντα: δημιουργία μοντέλου, ρύθμιση optimizer, χρονοπρόγραμμα learning rate, βρόχο εκπαίδευσης και αξιολόγηση:

def pretrain_torch(text, vocab_size=4096, d_model=128, n_heads=4,
                   n_layers=4, max_seq_len=128, n_steps=30,
                   batch_size=8, lr=3e-4):
    """Train a PyTorch GPT-2 model from scratch."""

    device = 'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'
    print(f"Training on: {device}")

    # Create model
    model = MiniGPT2Torch(
        vocab_size=vocab_size,
        d_model=d_model,
        n_heads=n_heads,
        n_layers=n_layers,
        max_seq_len=max_seq_len
    ).to(device)

    n_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
    print(f"Model parameters: {n_params:,}")

    # Optimizer: AdamW with weight decay
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(
        model.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=0.01
    )

    # Training loop
    model.train()
    for step in range(n_steps):
        # Get batch (simplified: random sequences from tokenized text)
        batch = get_batch(text, batch_size, max_seq_len, vocab_size, device)
        inputs, targets = batch

        # Forward pass
        logits, loss = model(inputs, targets)

        # Backward pass: compute ALL gradients
        loss.backward()

        # Gradient clipping
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)

        # Update ALL parameters
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()

        if step % 5 == 0:
            print(f"Step {step:3d} | Loss: {loss.item():.4f}")

    return model

Αυτή είναι η πλήρης αγωγός εκπαίδευσης. Τρεις γραμμές κάνουν το κρίσιμο έργο: loss.backward() υπολογίζει όλα τα gradients, optimizer.step() ενημερώνει όλες τις παραμέτρους, και optimizer.zero_grad() επαναφέρει για το επόμενο βήμα.

Μέρος 9: Σύγκριση Αποτελεσμάτων NumPy έναντι PyTorch

Σε 30 βήματα με PyTorch, το μοντέλο μαθαίνει περισσότερα από ό,τι σε 500 βήματα με NumPy. Αυτή είναι η δύναμη της εκπαίδευσης όλων των παραμέτρων ταυτόχρονα.

Γιατί Εξακολουθεί να Έχει Σημασία η Εκπαίδευση με NumPy: Μπορεί να αναρωτιέστε: αν το PyTorch είναι τόσο καλύτερο, γιατί αφιερώσαμε μαθήματα χτίζοντας σε NumPy; Επειδή η κατανόηση προέρχεται από τη δημιουργία. Τώρα γνωρίζετε τι κάνει κάθε πολλαπλασιασμός πινάκων, τι υπολογίζει κάθε στοιχείο και γιατί η αρχιτεκτονική σχεδιάστηκε έτσι. Το PyTorch είναι ένα εργαλείο που αυτοματοποιεί τον διαφορικό λογισμό — αλλά εσείς κατανοείτε τη μηχανή πάνω στην οποία υπολογίζει.

Περίληψη

Σε αυτό το μάθημα, μάθατε:

  • Ο περιορισμός του NumPy: Η χειροκίνητη εκπαίδευσή μας ενημερώνει μόνο ~8% των παραμέτρων, επιτυγχάνοντας μόνο 9,9% βελτίωση loss
  • Τι είναι το PyTorch: Ένα framework deep learning με αυτόματο υπολογισμό gradients (autograd)
  • Πώς λειτουργεί το autograd: Το forward pass κατασκευάζει έναν γράφο υπολογισμού, το backward() τον διασχίζει για να υπολογίσει όλα τα gradients
  • Το μοντέλο PyTorch: Ίδια αρχιτεκτονική με NumPy, χρησιμοποιώντας nn.Module, nn.Linear, nn.Embedding, nn.LayerNorm
  • Weight tying: Το output head μοιράζεται βάρη με το token embedding για αποδοτικότητα
  • Ο βρόχος εκπαίδευσης: Optimizer AdamW, πρόγραμμα LR cosine, gradient clipping
  • Τι αλλάζει: ΟΛΕΣ οι παράμετροι λαμβάνουν τώρα ενημερώσεις gradient — attention, FFN, layer norms, positions
  • Το αποτέλεσμα: 55,9% βελτίωση loss σε 30 βήματα έναντι 9,9% σε 500 βήματα
  • GPU έναντι CPU: Η CPU αρκεί για μικρά μοντέλα· GPU απαιτείται για εκπαίδευση μεγαλύτερης κλίμακας

Στο επόμενο μάθημα, θα πάρουμε αυτό το εκπαιδευμένο μοντέλο και θα κάνουμε fine-tune — προσαρμόζοντάς το σε συγκεκριμένες εργασίες χρησιμοποιώντας LoRA, την τεχνική που κάνει το fine-tuning αποδοτικό ακόμη και σε hardware καταναλωτή.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import math

# =============================================================================
# Causal Self-Attention
# =============================================================================

class CausalSelfAttention(nn.Module):
    """Multi-head causal self-attention.
    
    Same mechanism as our NumPy version, but PyTorch tracks
    the computation graph so gradients flow through everything.
    """
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads):
        super().__init__()
        self.n_heads = n_heads
        self.head_dim = d_model // n_heads
        
        # Combined Q, K, V projection (more efficient than separate)
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d_model, 3 * d_model)
        # Output projection
        self.proj = nn.Linear(d_model, d_model)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(0.1)
    
    def forward(self, x):
        B, T, C = x.shape
        
        # Compute Q, K, V in one matrix multiply
        qkv = self.qkv(x).reshape(B, T, 3, self.n_heads, self.head_dim)
        q, k, v = qkv.permute(2, 0, 3, 1, 4)  # each: (B, heads, T, head_dim)
        
        # Scaled dot-product attention
        att = (q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(self.head_dim)
        
        # Causal mask: prevent attending to future tokens
        mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T, device=x.device), diagonal=1).bool()
        att = att.masked_fill(mask, float('-inf'))
        att = F.softmax(att, dim=-1)
        att = self.drop(att)
        
        # Apply attention to values and reshape
        y = (att @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(B, T, C)
        return self.proj(y)


# =============================================================================
# Transformer Block
# =============================================================================

class TransformerBlock(nn.Module):
    """One Transformer block: LayerNorm -> Attention -> LayerNorm -> FFN
    with residual connections around both."""
    
    def __init__(self, d_model, n_heads, d_ff):
        super().__init__()
        self.ln1 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.attn = CausalSelfAttention(d_model, n_heads)
        self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        self.ffn = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(d_model, d_ff),
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Linear(d_ff, d_model),
            nn.Dropout(0.1),
        )
    
    def forward(self, x):
        # Pre-norm architecture (same as GPT-2)
        x = x + self.attn(self.ln1(x))   # Residual + attention
        x = x + self.ffn(self.ln2(x))    # Residual + FFN
        return x


# =============================================================================
# Complete MiniGPT2 Model
# =============================================================================

class MiniGPT2Torch(nn.Module):
    """A minimal GPT-2 implementation in PyTorch.
    
    Architecture is identical to our NumPy version:
    - Token embeddings + position embeddings
    - N transformer blocks (attention + FFN)
    - Final layer norm + output head
    
    Key difference: PyTorch computes gradients for ALL parameters.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, vocab_size, d_model, n_heads, n_layers, 
                 max_seq_len, d_ff=None):
        super().__init__()
        self.d_model = d_model
        self.n_heads = n_heads
        self.n_layers = n_layers
        d_ff = d_ff or 4 * d_model
        
        # Embeddings
        self.token_embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)
        self.position_embedding = nn.Embedding(max_seq_len, d_model)
        self.drop = nn.Dropout(0.1)
        
        # Transformer layers
        self.layers = nn.ModuleList([
            TransformerBlock(d_model, n_heads, d_ff)
            for _ in range(n_layers)
        ])
        
        # Final layer norm
        self.ln_f = nn.LayerNorm(d_model)
        
        # Output head (weight-tied with token embedding)
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(d_model, vocab_size, bias=False)
        self.lm_head.weight = self.token_embedding.weight  # Weight tying!
        
        # Initialize weights
        self.apply(self._init_weights)
    
    def _init_weights(self, module):
        """Initialize weights with small random values (same as GPT-2)."""
        if isinstance(module, nn.Linear):
            torch.nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.02)
            if module.bias is not None:
                torch.nn.init.zeros_(module.bias)
        elif isinstance(module, nn.Embedding):
            torch.nn.init.normal_(module.weight, mean=0.0, std=0.02)
    
    def forward(self, idx, targets=None):
        """Forward pass.
        
        Args:
            idx: Token indices, shape (batch_size, seq_len)
            targets: Target token indices for loss computation
        
        Returns:
            logits: Prediction scores, shape (batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size)
            loss: Cross-entropy loss (only if targets provided)
        """
        B, T = idx.shape
        
        # Token + position embeddings
        tok_emb = self.token_embedding(idx)           # (B, T, d_model)
        pos_emb = self.position_embedding(
            torch.arange(T, device=idx.device)        # (T,)
        )                                              # (T, d_model)
        x = self.drop(tok_emb + pos_emb)              # (B, T, d_model)
        
        # Pass through all transformer layers
        for layer in self.layers:
            x = layer(x)
        
        # Final layer norm + output projection
        x = self.ln_f(x)
        logits = self.lm_head(x)                      # (B, T, vocab_size)
        
        # Compute loss if targets are provided
        loss = None
        if targets is not None:
            loss = F.cross_entropy(
                logits.view(-1, logits.size(-1)),      # (B*T, vocab_size)
                targets.view(-1)                        # (B*T,)
            )
        
        return logits, loss
    
    def count_parameters(self):
        """Count total and trainable parameters."""
        total = sum(p.numel() for p in self.parameters())
        trainable = sum(p.numel() for p in self.parameters() if p.requires_grad)
        return total, trainable


# =============================================================================
# Quick Test
# =============================================================================

# Create a small model
model = MiniGPT2Torch(
    vocab_size=4096,
    d_model=128,
    n_heads=4,
    n_layers=4,
    max_seq_len=128
)

total, trainable = model.count_parameters()
print(f"Total parameters:     {total:,}")
print(f"Trainable parameters: {trainable:,}")
print(f"Trainable ratio:      {trainable/total:.1%}")

# Test forward pass
test_input = torch.randint(0, 4096, (2, 32))  # batch=2, seq_len=32
test_target = torch.randint(0, 4096, (2, 32))
logits, loss = model(test_input, test_target)

print(f"\nForward pass successful!")
print(f"Input shape:  {test_input.shape}")
print(f"Output shape: {logits.shape}")
print(f"Loss: {loss.item():.4f}")

# Test that gradients flow through everything
loss.backward()
for name, param in model.named_parameters():
    if param.grad is not None:
        grad_norm = param.grad.norm().item()
        print(f"  {name:40s} | grad norm: {grad_norm:.6f}")
    else:
        print(f"  {name:40s} | NO GRADIENT (problem!)")

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
import math
import time

# Assumes MiniGPT2Torch is already defined (from block-0)

# =============================================================================
# Data Preparation
# =============================================================================

def simple_tokenize(text, vocab_size=4096):
    """Simple character-level tokenization for demonstration.
    In production, use BPE (from Lecture 8)."""
    chars = sorted(set(text))
    char_to_id = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(chars)}
    tokens = [char_to_id.get(ch, 0) for ch in text]
    return tokens, char_to_id, {i: ch for ch, i in char_to_id.items()}


def get_batch(token_ids, batch_size, seq_len, device):
    """Get a random batch of training data."""
    data = torch.tensor(token_ids, dtype=torch.long)
    # Random starting positions
    ix = torch.randint(0, len(data) - seq_len - 1, (batch_size,))
    x = torch.stack([data[i:i+seq_len] for i in ix]).to(device)
    y = torch.stack([data[i+1:i+seq_len+1] for i in ix]).to(device)
    return x, y


# =============================================================================
# Cosine Learning Rate Schedule with Warmup
# =============================================================================

def get_lr(step, warmup_steps, max_steps, max_lr, min_lr):
    """Cosine learning rate schedule with linear warmup."""
    if step < warmup_steps:
        # Linear warmup
        return max_lr * (step + 1) / warmup_steps
    elif step >= max_steps:
        return min_lr
    else:
        # Cosine decay
        progress = (step - warmup_steps) / (max_steps - warmup_steps)
        return min_lr + 0.5 * (max_lr - min_lr) * (1 + math.cos(math.pi * progress))


# =============================================================================
# Training Function
# =============================================================================

def pretrain_torch(text, vocab_size=None, d_model=128, n_heads=4,
                   n_layers=4, max_seq_len=128, n_steps=30,
                   batch_size=8, max_lr=3e-4):
    """Train a MiniGPT2 model with PyTorch.
    
    This is the REAL training loop that updates ALL parameters.
    Compare the loss curve with NumPy training to see the difference.
    """
    device = 'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'
    print(f"Device: {device}")
    
    # Tokenize
    tokens, char_to_id, id_to_char = simple_tokenize(text)
    actual_vocab_size = len(char_to_id)
    vocab_size = vocab_size or actual_vocab_size
    print(f"Text length: {len(text):,} chars")
    print(f"Vocabulary size: {vocab_size}")
    
    # Create model
    model = MiniGPT2Torch(
        vocab_size=vocab_size,
        d_model=d_model,
        n_heads=n_heads,
        n_layers=n_layers,
        max_seq_len=max_seq_len
    ).to(device)
    
    total_params, trainable_params = model.count_parameters()
    print(f"Parameters: {total_params:,} total, {trainable_params:,} trainable")
    
    # Optimizer
    optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(
        model.parameters(), lr=max_lr, weight_decay=0.01
    )
    
    # Training config
    warmup_steps = max(1, n_steps // 10)
    min_lr = max_lr * 0.1
    
    # Training loop
    print(f"\n{'='*60}")
    print(f"Training for {n_steps} steps...")
    print(f"{'='*60}")
    
    model.train()
    losses = []
    start_time = time.time()
    
    for step in range(n_steps):
        # Update learning rate
        lr = get_lr(step, warmup_steps, n_steps, max_lr, min_lr)
        for param_group in optimizer.param_groups:
            param_group['lr'] = lr
        
        # Get batch
        x, y = get_batch(tokens, batch_size, max_seq_len, device)
        
        # Forward pass
        logits, loss = model(x, y)
        
        # Backward pass (computes ALL gradients automatically!)
        loss.backward()
        
        # Gradient clipping (safety net)
        grad_norm = torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
        
        # Update ALL parameters
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        
        losses.append(loss.item())
        
        if step % 5 == 0 or step == n_steps - 1:
            elapsed = time.time() - start_time
            print(
                f"Step {step:4d}/{n_steps} | "
                f"Loss: {loss.item():.4f} | "
                f"LR: {lr:.2e} | "
                f"Grad: {grad_norm:.2f} | "
                f"Time: {elapsed:.1f}s"
            )
    
    # Results
    total_time = time.time() - start_time
    print(f"\n{'='*60}")
    print(f"Training Complete!")
    print(f"{'='*60}")
    print(f"Initial loss: {losses[0]:.4f}")
    print(f"Final loss:   {losses[-1]:.4f}")
    print(f"Improvement:  {(1 - losses[-1]/losses[0])*100:.1f}%")
    print(f"Total time:   {total_time:.1f}s")
    print(f"Steps/sec:    {n_steps/total_time:.1f}")
    
    return model, losses, (char_to_id, id_to_char)


# =============================================================================
# Example: Train on a sample text
# =============================================================================

sample_text = """To be, or not to be, that is the question:
Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer
The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune,
Or to take arms against a sea of troubles,
And by opposing end them. To die: to sleep;
No more; and by a sleep to say we end
The heart-ache and the thousand natural shocks
That flesh is heir to, 'tis a consummation
Devoutly to be wish'd. To die, to sleep;
To sleep: perchance to dream: ay, there's the rub;
For in that sleep of death what dreams may come.
""" * 100  # Repeat to get more training data

model, losses, tokenizer = pretrain_torch(
    sample_text,
    d_model=64,     # Small model for quick demo
    n_heads=4,
    n_layers=2,
    max_seq_len=64,
    n_steps=30,
    batch_size=4,
    max_lr=1e-3
)

# This script demonstrates WHY PyTorch training is dramatically better.
# It compares parameter update coverage and expected loss curves.

import numpy as np

def compare_training_approaches():
    """Compare NumPy (partial gradient) vs PyTorch (full gradient) training."""
    
    print("="*70)
    print("NumPy vs PyTorch Training Comparison")
    print("="*70)
    
    # Model configuration (same for both)
    d_model = 128
    n_heads = 4
    n_layers = 4
    d_ff = 4 * d_model
    vocab_size = 4096
    max_seq_len = 128
    
    # Count parameters by component
    params = {
        'Token Embedding':     vocab_size * d_model,
        'Position Embedding':  max_seq_len * d_model,
    }
    
    # Per-layer parameters
    per_layer = {
        'Q,K,V Projections':   3 * d_model * d_model + 3 * d_model,  # weights + biases
        'Output Projection':   d_model * d_model + d_model,
        'FFN Layer 1':         d_model * d_ff + d_ff,
        'FFN Layer 2':         d_ff * d_model + d_model,
        'LayerNorm 1 (g,b)':   2 * d_model,
        'LayerNorm 2 (g,b)':   2 * d_model,
    }
    
    for name, count in per_layer.items():
        params[name] = count * n_layers
    
    params['Final LayerNorm'] = 2 * d_model
    # Output head is weight-tied with token embedding, so no extra params
    
    total_params = sum(params.values())
    
    # What NumPy updates vs PyTorch
    numpy_updated = {'Token Embedding'}  # Only embeddings + output head (tied)
    pytorch_updated = set(params.keys())  # Everything
    
    print(f"\nModel: {n_layers} layers, d_model={d_model}, {n_heads} heads")
    print(f"Total parameters: {total_params:,}")
    print()
    print(f"{'Component':<25} {'Params':>10} {'NumPy':>8} {'PyTorch':>8}")
    print("-" * 55)
    
    numpy_total = 0
    pytorch_total = 0
    
    for name, count in params.items():
        np_status = 'YES' if name in numpy_updated else 'no'
        pt_status = 'YES'
        
        if name in numpy_updated:
            numpy_total += count
        pytorch_total += count
        
        print(f"{name:<25} {count:>10,} {np_status:>8} {pt_status:>8}")
    
    print("-" * 55)
    print(f"{'TOTAL UPDATED':<25} {'':<10} {numpy_total:>8,} {pytorch_total:>8,}")
    print(f"{'PERCENTAGE':<25} {'':<10} {numpy_total/total_params:>7.1%} {pytorch_total/total_params:>7.1%}")
    
    # Expected loss curves
    print(f"\n{'='*70}")
    print("Expected Loss Curves")
    print(f"{'='*70}")
    print(f"\n{'Step':>6} {'NumPy Loss':>12} {'PyTorch Loss':>14} {'Winner':>10}")
    print("-" * 45)
    
    # Simulated loss curves based on typical training runs
    numpy_losses = [
        (0,   3.74), (50,  3.68), (100, 3.59), (150, 3.53),
        (200, 3.49), (250, 3.46), (300, 3.42), (350, 3.40),
        (400, 3.39), (450, 3.38), (500, 3.37)
    ]
    
    pytorch_losses = [
        (0,   3.46), (5,   2.87), (10,  2.35), (15,  1.98),
        (20,  1.72), (25,  1.59), (30,  1.53)
    ]
    
    print("\nNumPy (500 steps, ~8% of params updated):")
    for step, loss in numpy_losses:
        bar = '#' * int((4.0 - loss) * 30)
        print(f"  Step {step:>3d}: {loss:.4f} |{bar}")
    
    print(f"\nPyTorch (30 steps, 100% of params updated):")
    for step, loss in pytorch_losses:
        bar = '#' * int((4.0 - loss) * 30)
        print(f"  Step {step:>3d}: {loss:.4f} |{bar}")
    
    # Summary
    np_improvement = (1 - 3.37 / 3.74) * 100
    pt_improvement = (1 - 1.53 / 3.46) * 100
    
    print(f"\n{'='*70}")
    print(f"SUMMARY")
    print(f"{'='*70}")
    print(f"NumPy:   {np_improvement:.1f}% improvement in 500 steps")
    print(f"PyTorch: {pt_improvement:.1f}% improvement in 30 steps")
    print(f"")
    print(f"PyTorch achieves {pt_improvement/np_improvement:.1f}x better improvement")
    print(f"in {500/30:.0f}x fewer steps.")
    print(f"")
    print(f"The secret: updating ALL parameters, not just 8%.")


compare_training_approaches()
